title: CHEM1A Practice Quiz — Objective 8: Bonding I — Lewis, VSEPR, Valence Bond (DRAFT pending Gilley approval)

items.stem: Which pair of elements forms an ionic bond?
items.explain: Metal + nonmetal transfers electrons — ionic. The other three pairs are nonmetal + nonmetal: they share, making covalent bonds.

items.stem: Which compound has the LARGEST lattice energy?
choices: SrS — 2+ and 2−, but larger anion than SrO
items.explain: Charge product first: the 2+/2− pairs beat every 1+/1− pair. Size second: between SrO and SrS, oxide is smaller than sulfide, so SrO's ions sit closer. Checking size before charge is the classic inversion.

items.stem: Which bond is the MOST polar? (EN: B = 2.0, C = 2.5, N = 3.0, O = 3.5)
items.explain: Bond polarity rides on the electronegativity DIFFERENCE: the partner farthest from oxygen makes the most lopsided pair. O–O is perfectly nonpolar.

items.stem: In a polar covalent bond, the shared electrons:
choices: Spend more time near the more electronegative atom
Sit exactly halfway between the nuclei at all times
items.explain: Polar covalent = uneven sharing, not transfer. Complete transfer is ionic; perfectly even sharing is nonpolar covalent.

items.stem: How many total valence electrons belong in the Lewis structure of PF₃?
items.explain: 5 (P) + 3 × 7 (F) = 26. The count comes FIRST — 24 forgets phosphorus's lone pair allotment (miscounting P as 3); 8 counts only one atom's octet.

items.stem: How many total valence electrons belong in the Lewis structure of the bromate ion, BrO₃⁻?
items.explain: 7 (Br) + 3 × 6 (O) + 1 (the ion's −1 charge) = 26. The charge enters at the count step — 25 is the count with the charge forgotten, the single most common ion error.

items.stem: How many total valence electrons belong in the Lewis structure of ethanol, C₂H₅OH?
items.explain: 2 × 4 (C) + 6 × 1 (H) + 6 (O) = 8 + 6 + 6 = 20. The count comes FIRST, even for organics — 22 hands oxygen a full octet instead of its six valence electrons; 14 forgets the six hydrogens entirely.

items.stem: In the correct Lewis structure of methylamine, CH₃NH₂ (skeleton H₃C–NH₂), the nitrogen atom carries:
items.explain: Count first: 4 (C) + 5 (N) + 5 × 1 (H) = 14 electrons. Six bonds place 12 of them; the last pair sits on nitrogen as its one lone pair, completing its octet. Two lone pairs is oxygen's pattern misapplied; a C=N double bond would overfill both octets here.

items.stem: What is the formal charge on the carbon of CH₃⁻ (three C–H bonds and one lone pair on carbon)?
items.explain: FC = valence − (nonbonding + ½ bonding) = 4 − (2 + 3) = −1 — which matches the ion's charge, the built-in self-check. 0 forgets the lone pair; −4 subtracts everything from nothing.

items.stem: When two Lewis structures are otherwise equally good, the better one places any NEGATIVE formal charge on:
items.explain: Negative charge belongs where electrons are most welcome — the most electronegative atom. That tiebreak (after minimizing charges) picks the real skeleton in cases like cyanate.

items.stem: The two carbon-oxygen bonds of the formate ion, HCO₂⁻, are exactly equal in length. This is because the ion:
choices: Is a resonance hybrid — one averaged structure with two identical intermediate bonds
Flickers rapidly between its two Lewis structures
items.explain: The hybrid is a permanent average, not a movie. Flickering would still show one short and one long bond at any instant; the equal lengths are the fingerprint of the average.

items.stem: In the acetate ion, CH₃COO⁻, how many equivalent positions can the carbon-oxygen double bond occupy?
items.explain: The double bond has two legal homes — one per oxygen — giving two resonance structures and two identical carbon-oxygen bonds in the real ion.

items.stem: Which molecule CANNOT satisfy the octet rule for every atom, no matter how you draw it?
items.explain: NO₂ has 17 valence electrons — an odd number. Pairs can never cover an odd count, so one electron stays unpaired. Check the count before drawing a single dot.

items.stem: Which element can hold MORE than eight electrons in its valence shell?
choices: Sulfur — period 3, with d orbitals available
Nitrogen — it has five valence electrons
items.explain: Expanded octets need an empty d subshell in the valence shell — available from period 3 down. Nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine live in period 2 (n = 2 holds only s and p) and never exceed eight.

items.stem: What is the molecular geometry of PH₃ (three bonds and one lone pair on phosphorus)?
items.explain: Four electron groups → tetrahedral ELECTRON geometry; the lone pair keeps its seat but drops out of the name → trigonal pyramidal MOLECULAR geometry. Tetrahedral is the electron-geometry answer put in the wrong blank.

items.stem: Which molecule is LINEAR?
items.explain: BeF₂ has two electron groups and no lone pairs on beryllium → linear, 180°. H₂O and OF₂ are bent (their lone pairs fold them); NH₃ is trigonal pyramidal.

items.stem: Which molecule is NONPOLAR even though its bonds are polar?
items.explain: SiF₄'s perfect tetrahedron of four IDENTICAL bonds cancels the four dipole arrows. The others are asymmetric — bent, mixed corners, or lone-pair-tilted — and keep a net arrow.

items.stem: A bent molecule whose two bonds are polar is:
choices: Always polar — dipoles at an angle cannot fully cancel
Polar only if it contains oxygen
Impossible to classify without measuring it
items.explain: Cancellation requires arrows pointing exactly opposite; a bend guarantees they do not. Shape plus bond dipoles decides polarity — nothing about oxygen specifically.

items.stem: Which carbon-carbon bond is the SHORTEST?
choices: They are all the same length
items.explain: Bond order up → length down (and energy up). Triple bonds pull the same two atoms closest together.

items.stem: For bonds between the same two atoms, as bond order increases from single to triple, bond energy:
choices: Increases — more shared pairs bind more strongly
items.explain: Order up → energy up, length down: three rungs of the same ladder. This pairing (stronger AND shorter) is the pattern the final tests.

items.stem: Which alkene exists as cis and trans isomers?
items.explain: Cis/trans needs two DIFFERENT groups on EACH carbon of the double bond. In the other three, at least one double-bond carbon carries two identical groups — swap them and nothing changes.

items.stem: How many degrees of unsaturation does C₆H₁₀ have?
items.explain: (2 × 6 + 2 − 10)/2 = 2 — some combination of two rings and π bonds. 1 miscounts the hydrogens; 0 describes the saturated C₆H₁₄.

items.stem: A triple bond consists of:
choices: One σ bond and two π bonds
Two σ bonds and one π bond
items.explain: Every bond gets exactly one head-on σ; the extra lines are side-on π bonds. Three σ bonds between the same two atoms is geometrically impossible.

items.stem: A π bond forms when two orbitals overlap:
choices: Side-on, above and below the line between the nuclei
Head-on, along the line between the nuclei
Not at all — π bonds are ionic
items.explain: Side-on p-orbital overlap is the π signature — and it is why rotation (which would tear the side-on contact apart) is locked. Head-on overlap is the σ bond.

items.stem: What is the hybridization of the carbon atom in CH₃Cl (four single bonds, no lone pairs)?
items.explain: Four electron groups → sp³ → tetrahedral. The lookup runs count → hybridization: 2 groups sp, 3 groups sp², 4 groups sp³.

items.stem: An sp-hybridized central atom is surrounded by how many electron groups, in what arrangement?
items.explain: sp mixes two orbitals for two groups at 180° — and leaves two unhybridized p orbitals, which is how a triple bond's two π bonds fit.

items.stem: Electronegativity is:
choices: An atom's pull on the electrons it SHARES in a bond
The energy needed to remove an electron from an isolated atom
The number of valence electrons an atom has
items.explain: Pull on SHARED electrons — a bonding property. The remove-an-electron definition is ionization energy (Objective 7's trend, a close cousin but a different measurement).

items.stem: Bond energy is:
choices: The energy required to break one mole of that bond in the gas phase
The energy stored inside the bonded atoms' nuclei
The heat released when any bond breaks
The mass difference between bonded and free atoms
items.explain: Breaking bonds always COSTS energy (bond energies are positive); heat is released only when stronger bonds FORM. 'Breaking releases energy' is the misconception the ΔH-from-bond-energies method exposes.
